newsitem.title: USA: Stage set for dynamic changes on Korea peninsula.
newsitem.headline: Stage set for dynamic changes on Korea peninsula.

text.p: The stage is set for a radical change on the Korean peninsula if Pyongyang, as expected, finally agrees this week to begin four-party peace talks with rival South Korea, the United States and China.

The landmark negotiations are not actually expected to get under way until June or July. They aim to defuse tensions on the heavily armed and volatile peninsula and close the books on the 1950-53 Korean War that sealed the division between north and south by replacing the amistice with a peace treaty.

U.S. officials are optimistic that barring some unforseen crisis, North Korea will tell the United States and South Korea at a meeting on Wednesday in New York it is prepared finally to open the peace talks, as allies Seoul and Washington proposed one year ago.

The talks hold the promise for North Korea's Stalinist regime of reviving an economically ravaged country in which thousands of people face famine, of clinging to power -- at least in the short run -- and of achieving coveted legitimacy from the United States.

But as often is the case with Pyongyang, "yes" may not come easily. "I think the North Koreans are congenitally unable to finish off a deal until they absolutely have rung every last bit of advantage out of it," a U.S. official said.

"That's understandable but they can't afford to walk away and we're probably going to spend hours on Wednesday convincing them that there is no further advantage to be gained" from withholding assent to the peace talks, the official told Reuters.
This may mean the meeting has to be carried over until Friday, but "once we have done that, I think they will give us an unequivocal yes," the official said in an interview.

It is expected North Korea will make a final pitch for massive food aid to compensate for two years of shortages due to flooding that the United States, as well as humanitarian groups, agree are devastating and worsening.
To pre-empt that, Washington would announce another donation of food aid, in addition to $18.4 million provided since late 1995, including $10 million enroute to North Korea.

Humanitarian groups say another $10 million contribution will be inadequate. Some assert Washington should provide at least $40 million total, nearly half of the World Food Program's current appeal for $95.5 million or 200,000 tons of food out of a projected North Korean need of 2 million tons.

The United States insists it has not used food as a weapon in the political duel with North Korea, which Washington believes has at least two nuclear devices, plus a 1.3 million man army with artillery arrayed against 37,000 American troops and their South Korean allies on the peninsula.
But officials have made clear Pyongyang is unlikely to receive anywhere near the total amount of food or other assistance it needs until it takes steps to reduce tensions.
"I doubt very much whether there will be massive assistance without some kind of reciprocal action on the part of the North Koreans," Defence Secretary William Cohen said last week.

Republican Sen. Ted Stevens, just returned from Pyongyang, said Washington should ease restrictions on commercial food sales to relieve the starvation threat. But he also told the North Koreans "military tensions must be reduced to facilitate progress on food, energy and other concerns."
Critics accuse the administration doing too much or doing too little, of propping a Stalinist system or failing to deliver promised help that would foster gradual change there.
Officials believe it is in the U.S. self-interest not to let North Korea implode, unleashing instability, massive refugees flows and unpredictable reactions from Pyongyang.

But Asia expert Selig Harrison says Washington is far from advocating a "soft landing" strategy that promotes a gradual unification of North and South and helps Pyongyang achieve a China-like economic tranformation.

He argues that instead of demanding that North Korea first take demilitarization steps, for instance, Washington should propose a comprehensive deal in which it would promise guaranteed food aid and an easing of U.S. trade sanctions, in return for Pyongyang's commitment to redeploy troops and arms.
